evidence_quotes.quote: We analyze in-depth, semi-structured interviews with managers and key informants from 11 publicly owned water utilities in Massachusetts and Pennsylvania to examine (1) how interviewees invoke environmentality values and prosocial values when discussing water affordability, and (2) whether those values translate into concrete policies that advance distributive, procedural, or recognition justice for customers who cannot afford to pay their bills.

For some utilities, uniform rates and strict collection practices reflect a value of disciplinary power, justified through a narrow understanding of fairness that sidesteps recognition of unequal burden and punishes people for unpaid bills.

Most utility personnel signaled a willingness to waive interest or fees but were reluctant to forgive the principal charge. In only a few Benevolence-Led utilities would officials erase debt in negotiating a payment plan with a customer.

Between 2020 and 2022, we conducted 33 semi-structured interviews with 37 informants across the 11 cities. Using purposive sampling, we identified individuals most likely to hold knowledge of rate-setting and affordability policy:

defend uniform rates as the only just option, invoking tradition, conformity to peer prices, and fiscal security to explain why all customers must pay the same for water and no customer’s debt can be forgiven. Four cities in our sample fell into this category.

Utility managers in these places reject the idea that fairness must entail uniformity. They embed procedural justice in their organizations by consulting their most vulnerable customers and the advocates who work with them in designing rate structures and assistance plans.

criterion_notes.c1: Examines household drinking-water service affordability, billing, customer assistance programs (CAPs), debt relief, and collection/shutoff practices across 11 publicly owned municipal water utilities in Massachusetts and Pennsylvania.
criterion_notes.c2: Passes BOTH the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2 (with a borderline note on framing). Under the plain wording, it clearly examines municipal utility governance, organizational culture/values, regulatory pressures, and CAP administration. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading, although the overarching theoretical construct is organizational values (Schwartz human values typology), the empirical analysis directly examines how core rule-type mechanisms govern affordability and access to relief: tariff and cost-recovery rules (ascending block rates, strict rate uniformity, refusal to abate principal charges even on leaks, consultant rate benchmarking, state regulatory agency rate approvals, and Safe Drinking Water Act compliance cost pass-through), street-level discretion and accommodation (waiving interest/fees, flex-pay payment plans, principal debt erasure, ad-hoc hardship grants), eligibility screening and administrative burden in CAPs (differential discounts by senior/low-income status, simplified enrollment, outreach clinics), enforcement (aggressive collections, fines, liens, shutoffs), and perceived municipal legal constraints on differential pricing.
criterion_notes.c3: Primary qualitative socio-legal empirical study based on 33 semi-structured interviews with 37 utility managers, staff, board members, and municipal officials across 11 cities (2020-2022), analyzed using hybrid inductive-deductive coding in Dedoose. Qualitative socio-legal studies are explicitly eligible for the mechanism synthesis.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports qualitative utility-level outcomes directly governing household water affordability, accommodation, and exclusion from relief across the 11 cities (categorized into 4 Traditionalist utilities enforcing strict uniform rates and collections without debt forgiveness, 5 Balancer utilities providing ad-hoc fee waivers, payment plans, and small hardship grants, and 2 Benevolence-Led utilities providing targeted status/income-based CAP discounts, debt erasure, and simplified enrollment/outreach). Note that direct household-level bill burden, CAP enrollment demographics, and shutoff counts are not quantitatively measured (acknowledged as a limitation on PDF p. 13).
criterion_notes.c5: Population/unit of analysis (11 municipal water utilities / cities in MA and PA; 37 interviewees), institutional/rule-type and cultural exposures, utility-level affordability/accommodation outcomes, and qualitative cross-case interview study design are all clearly identifiable.

study_design: Qualitative comparative cross-case study using semi-structured interviews (hybrid inductive-deductive thematic and content analysis)
population_and_sample: 11 publicly owned municipal water utilities (cities as unit of analysis) in Massachusetts and Pennsylvania; 33 semi-structured interviews with 37 informants (utility directors, finance managers, customer-service leads, municipal managers/finance officers, water commission/board members, and elected officials)
exposure: Organizational value orientations (environmentality and prosocial values) operating through rule-type utility mechanisms: tariff and cost-recovery rules (ascending block rates, uniform rate strictness, state regulatory rate filings, Safe Drinking Water Act compliance cost recovery), street-level discretion and accommodation (fee/interest waivers, flex-pay plans, principal debt abatement), Customer Assistance Program (CAP) eligibility/enrollment rules, perceived legal constraints, and collection enforcement
outcome: Utility-level household water affordability policies and practices across 11 cities: adoption vs denial of targeted CAP rate discounts (by low-income/senior status), principal debt forgiveness/abatement, fee/interest waivers, flex-pay plans, and simplified enrollment/outreach versus strict uniform cost recovery and punitive collections
rationale: This qualitative socio-legal empirical study (33 interviews with 37 officials/staff across 11 municipal water utilities in Massachusetts and Pennsylvania) satisfies all inclusion criteria for the systematic review's mechanism synthesis. Although framed around organizational values (Schwartz's typology), it empirically examines concrete rule-type mechanisms under the 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 scope — including tariff and cost-recovery rules (ascending block rates, strict uniform pricing, non-abatement of principal charges even for leaks, consultant benchmarking, and state regulatory rate filings), street-level discretion and accommodation (waiving fees/interest, flex-pay plans, principal debt erasure, hardship grants), CAP eligibility discounts and enrollment outreach, perceived legal constraints on differential rates, and punitive collection enforcement — and links them to utility-level water affordability and relief/exclusion practices across the 11 cities. Confidence is rated medium because the primary explanatory lens is organizational culture/values and outcomes are captured at the utility policy/practice level rather than direct household-level affordability or shutoff rates.
